teaser: Italy's most romantic picture is also a coded political poster. The clue is in the colors.
review_notes:
Hayez born February 1791, so 68 when the painting was shown in September 1859.
Commission by Count Alfonso Maria Visconti di Saliceto, bequeathed to the Brera in 1886.
Reading of the colors as the Italian and French flags (widely accepted but an interpretation, not a statement by Hayez).
Later versions: one with the woman in white (1861) is commonly cited; I only say 'later versions' changed the colors.
Perugina's Baci chocolate box of the 1920s (design by Federico Seneca) inspired by this painting.
Luchino Visconti's film Senso (1954) restaging the kiss.
The dagger hilt at the man's hip and the green lining of his cloak are small in this image: please check the spots.

lesson.text: 68. That is the age of the man who painted the most famous kiss in Italian art. Francesco Hayez was a white-haired professor at the Brera academy in Milan, born in Venice before Napoleon ever crossed the Alps. In 1859 he gave his country an image of young love that it has never stopped reproducing.

The scene is simple to describe. In the corner of a medieval building, a man in a cloak and feathered hat kisses a woman in a blue silk dress. We see neither face properly. His is under the brim of his hat, hers is hidden by his cheek and her own hair. Because they are nobody in particular, they can be anybody.

Now the date matters. In June 1859, French and Piedmontese troops drove the Austrian army out of Milan, which Austria had ruled for decades. Three months later Hayez showed this canvas at the Brera. Italy was not yet one country. People were fighting to make it one, with France as their ally. The costumes are medieval, but the colors are news.

lesson.title: Reading the colors
lesson.text: Follow four patches of color across the two bodies.

spots.title: Red
spots.text: His tights are a loud, unbroken red. Hayez keeps the cloak dull brown so that this red jumps out from underneath.

spots.title: Green
spots.text: At the collar and near her wrist, the lining of his cloak shows: a sliver of bright green. It is tiny, and it is no accident.

spots.title: White
spots.text: Her puffed undersleeve is white. Red, green, white: together the lovers wear the three colors of the Italian flag.

spots.title: Blue
spots.text: And the dress? With the white and the red it also spells out the blue, white and red of France. The embrace joins two flags. The alliance is sealed with a kiss.

lesson.text: Hayez hides a political message inside a love scene: the couple's clothes carry the colors of Italy and of its ally, France.

The painting was ordered by a Milanese count, Alfonso Maria Visconti di Saliceto, who kept it at home for a quarter of a century. He left it to the Brera gallery when he died, and it has hung there since 1886.

A flag alone would not move anyone. What makes the picture work is that this kiss is a goodbye. Look at his body: one hand holds her head, but his left foot is already on the first stair. He is half turned to leave. At his hip, the handle of a dagger pokes out from the cloak. Viewers in 1859 understood at once: a volunteer, off to fight.

She knows it too. She bends backward and grips his shoulder as if to hold him one second longer. The whole painting leans, from her trailing hem at bottom left up to his hat. And they may not be alone in this hallway.
Someone else is in the building. Search the darkest part of the picture.

spots.title: The shadow
spots.text: Through the archway, a dark figure stands at the foot of some stairs. A spy? A comrade waiting for him? A servant? Hayez never said. The uncertainty is what makes the kiss feel stolen.

lesson.text: That shadow turns a pose into a story with a before and an after. Hayez learned this from the theater and from opera, which Milan adored. He was the leading Italian painter of Romanticism, the movement that put feeling ahead of rules, and he often set modern passions in the Middle Ages so they could pass the Austrian censors.

The dress is the technical showpiece. To paint satin, Hayez laid sharp strokes of nearly pure white on the crests of the folds, next to deep gray-blue in the hollows. Visitors at the Brera still lean in to see whether the fabric is real.

Hayez painted the subject again several times for other buyers, changing the colors of the clothes as politics shifted. But the 1859 canvas is the one Italians took to heart. Within a few years it stood for the Risorgimento, the long struggle that produced a united Italy in 1861.

Its afterlife is sweet in every sense. In the 1920s the chocolate maker Perugina based the embracing couple on its Baci box (“baci” means kisses) on Hayez's lovers. In 1954 the director Luchino Visconti restaged the pose in his film Senso.

quiz.question: How old was Hayez when he showed The Kiss?
quiz.explanation: He was a 68-year-old professor at the Brera academy.

quiz.question: Which two flags do the couple's clothes bring together?
quiz.explanation: Red, green and white for Italy, and blue, white and red for its ally France.

quiz.question: What tells us the man is about to leave?
options: His foot is already on the stair
quiz.explanation: His left foot rests on the first step and his body is half turned away.

quiz.question: What is hidden in the dark archway on the left?
quiz.explanation: A dark figure stands at the foot of some stairs, and Hayez never explained who it is.

quiz.question: Where has the painting hung since 1886?
options: The Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan
quiz.explanation: The count who ordered it left it to the Brera.

facts.text: We can clearly see the faces of both lovers.
facts.explanation: His face is under his hat brim and hers is hidden by his cheek and her hair.

facts.text: The painting was first shown three months after Austrian troops were driven out of Milan.
facts.explanation: The Austrians left in June 1859 and Hayez exhibited the canvas that September.

facts.text: The costumes show the fashion of 1859.
facts.explanation: The clothes and setting are medieval, a way to speak about the present in disguise.
